definition: Argüman is a free and open source software for collective structured argumentation and argument analysis via argumentation graphs or argument maps in which the type of connections can be specified.
details: It allows users to create collaborative "semantic maps" of arguments in well structured tree formats and share them with an audience and potential participants. Arguman.org was an open structured social debate platform that implemented the software. It is down as of 2023. There also is a mobile version of the tool. The project was started, in 2014, and largely built by developers in Turkey. Some studies used or investigated excerpts of argumentations on the platform. Unlike the larger and functional alternative Kialo, which is structured using only 'Pro' and 'Con' relations, argüman arguments are structured by three types of premises – 'because', 'but', and 'however'. As of the latest version, debates are presented in their entirety as a large tree which may be harder to navigate than other formats – for instance, trees "can become extremely dense, and the interface does not make it obvious which arguments the user should pay attention to". Users can also flag arguments for fallacies. Arguman.org also had a Turkish-language subdomain. A researcher suggested the concept of the Semantic Web-interoperability could be useful for argumentative structures on the Web, going beyond the con

explainer.lead: Argüman is free, open-source software for building and examining arguments together as structured maps. It helps people see not just whether someone supports a claim, but how each premise supports, challenges, or qualifies it.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a big class discussion drawn as a tree instead of a long chat. The main idea sits at the top, and everyone adds reasons underneath using labels such as “because,” “but,” and “however.” This makes it easier to see how the parts of an argument fit together, although a very large tree can become crowded.
tiers.practitioner: Users collaboratively construct argument trees, connect premises with one of three relation types, share the resulting maps, and flag suspected fallacies. A mobile version exists, while Arguman.org, the social debate platform implementing the software, was down as of 2023. Dense trees can be difficult to navigate because the interface gives limited guidance about which arguments deserve attention.
tiers.paperLevel: A debate is represented as an argumentation graph or tree with a central claim, premise nodes, and directed connections typed “because,” “but,” or “however”; users can additionally annotate arguments with fallacy flags. This offers finer relation types than Kialo’s Pro/Con structure, but presenting an entire debate as one large tree can create dense, poorly prioritized views. Researchers have used or investigated excerpts of argumentation from the platform.

explainer.example: For the claim “Our town should add protected bicycle lanes,” a participant might add “because safer lanes can encourage cycling,” another might add “but construction would reduce road space,” and a third might add “however, that cost could be smaller on selected streets.” The map records these different roles instead of reducing every response to a simple pro or con.

explainer.intuition: A normal comment thread shows who replied to whom; Argüman shows what each statement does to the argument. Its three connection labels turn a debate into a visible structure of support, objection, and qualification.
howItWorks: A participant states the claim to be debated.
Users add premises and label their connections “because,” “but,” or “however.”
Further premises extend the discussion into a collaborative tree or semantic map.
Participants can flag arguments they believe contain fallacies.
The completed debate can be shared with an audience and potential contributors.
explainer.whyItMatters: It gives collaborative debate an inspectable structure, making relationships between claims easier to analyze than in an unstructured discussion. The project also provided material for studies of online argumentation.
misconceptions: Argüman is not limited to “Pro” and “Con”; it uses “because,” “but,” and “however” premise relations.
Flagging a fallacy marks a concern for inspection; it does not automatically settle whether an argument is valid.
Argüman and Arguman.org are not identical: one is the software, while the other was a platform implementing it.
